report.executive_summary: Between 2023 and 2024, Goldman Sachs demonstrated a significant operational and financial recovery characterized by a 16% increase in net revenues to $53.51 billion and a 68% surge in net earnings to $14.28 billion. This financial improvement coincided with a strategic restructuring that included the exit from consumer point-of-sale financing (GreenSky), the divestiture of the Personal Financial Management (PFM) business, and the introduction of a new Platform Solutions segment focused on partnership-based credit issuance. Concurrently, the company resolved numerous historical legal liabilities, including a $65 million CFPB settlement, the dismissal of the 1MDB DPA, and settlements in various underwriting litigations, thereby reducing contingent legal risks. Disclosure practices underwent substantial modification: while risk narratives expanded to include granular geopolitical, cyber, and AI-specific threats, key financial transparency metrics such as the Allowance for Credit Losses rollforward and segment-level operating expense detail were removed, shifting to a consolidated reporting view.
report.longitudinal_analysis: The transition from 2023 to 2024 involved a shift from resolving legacy operational issues and legal exposures to establishing new strategic structures and heightened risk awareness. Legally, the firm moved from an active cooperation status in the CFPB investigation and pending class actions in 2023 to definitive resolutions in 2024, including the $65 million CFPB settlement and the dismissal of the 1MDB DPA. Operationally, the firm narrowed its consumer footprint by exiting the GreenSky partnership and ceasing unsecured installment loan commitments, while simultaneously launching a new Platform Solutions segment centered on the Apple Card and GM programs. In terms of human capital, the company reversed its previous reduction-in-force trend, growing headcount by 3% in 2024 compared to a 7% reduction in 2023, though this was accompanied by the removal of specific senior executive profiles from public disclosures. Risk disclosure evolved from general warnings to detailed, specific articulations of geopolitical (tariffs, regional conflicts), regulatory (SCB framework changes, AI compliance), and operational (cyber, settlement failures) risks, reflecting an increasingly complex external environment.

key_findings.title: Final Resolution of CFPB Investigation with $65 Million Settlement
key_findings.analysis: In 2024, Goldman Sachs resolved its CFPB investigation into credit card account management practices by paying a $45 million penalty and providing approximately $20 million in restitution. This changes the disclosure from an ongoing cooperation status in 2023 to a definitive legal conclusion with fully paid financial losses, eliminating the previous contingency risk.

key_findings.title: Reversal of Litigation Dismissal and Subsequent Settlement
key_findings.analysis: The legal status of the Sea Limited underwriting litigation shifted materially in 2024. While the case was dismissed with prejudice in 2023, the Appellate Division reversed this dismissal in May 2024. Although the matter was settled in principle in November 2024 without contribution from GS Asia, the reversal resurrected legal uncertainty and liability exposure that was not present in the prior year's final dismissal.

key_findings.title: Removal of Critical Credit Risk and Liquidity Disclosures
key_findings.analysis: The 2024 filing removed several material quantitative disclosures present in 2023, including the Allowance for Credit Losses (ACL) rollforward table, specific collateralized financing balances (Resale agreements, Securities borrowed/loaned), and the net interest income volume/rate variance analysis. The removal of these items significantly reduces the transparency of the firm's credit exposure, liquidity positioning, and the drivers of net interest income.

key_findings.title: Consolidation of Operating Expenses to Firmwide Total
key_findings.analysis: The disclosure of operating expenses shifted from a segment-level view ($18.04 billion for Global Banking & Markets in 2023) to the consolidated firmwide total ($33.77 billion in 2024). This structural change in reporting scope alters the magnitude and context of the financial metric, moving from divisional performance to enterprise-wide results.

key_findings.title: Strategic Reorganization and Capital Structure Changes
key_findings.analysis: Two major structural changes occurred: the formation of the Capital Solutions Group in January 2025 to expand financing and risk management capabilities for financial sponsors, and the redemption of $2.2 billion in outstanding Series K and Series P Preferred Stock. The latter permanently altered the equity structure and removed preferred stock obligations.

key_findings.title: Granular Disclosure of Geopolitical and Cyber Risks
key_findings.analysis: Geopolitical risk disclosures were expanded from a single consolidated paragraph in 2023 into eight distinct disclosures in 2024. The 2024 filing specifically highlights risks related to the Russia-Ukraine conflict, Middle East tensions, US-China tensions, and China-Taiwan conflicts, while explicitly adding 'cyber attacks' and 'settlement failures' as potential consequences of conflict escalation, indicating heightened operational and compliance exposures.

key_findings.title: Final Settlement of $215 Million Employment Discrimination Class Action
key_findings.analysis: The specific disclosure regarding the $215 million settlement for the female employee discrimination class action was removed in 2024, indicating the settlement was fully executed. This represents a material change in legal posture by resolving a significant liability that was active in the 2023 period.

key_findings.title: Significant Reversal in Profitability and Revenue Drivers
key_findings.analysis: Goldman Sachs reported a substantial improvement in financial performance in 2024 compared to 2023. Net earnings increased by approximately 68% to $14.28 billion, with diluted EPS rising to $40.54 from $22.87. Total consolidated net revenues grew 16% to $53.51 billion, reversing the 2% decline seen in 2023. This recovery was driven by a fundamental shift in revenue sources: while 2023 relied on 'other principal transactions' to offset declines in net interest and investment banking, 2024 saw growth across all major pillars, with 'other principal transactions' doubling to $4.65 billion due to private equity and funding derivatives. This indicates a broad-based operational recovery rather than isolated gains.

key_findings.title: Strategic Narrowing of Consumer Platform Focus
key_findings.analysis: The company executed a strategic consolidation within its Platform Solutions segment in 2024, explicitly narrowing its focus on consumer-related activities. This involved the exit from the GreenSky point-of-sale financing partnership, which was present in the 2023 disclosures, and a reduction of consumer activities to primarily Apple Card credit card/deposit issuance and the GM credit card program. This structural change aligns with the 3% headcount growth in Asset & Wealth Management and Risk/Compliance, suggesting a reallocation of resources from discontinued consumer ventures to core wealth management and risk functions.

key_findings.title: Shift in Human Capital and Senior Leadership
key_findings.analysis: There was a marked reversal in workforce trends, moving from a 7% headcount reduction in 2023 (driven by reduction initiatives) to a 3% increase in 2024. Concurrently, the 2024 filings exhibit a removal of specific senior executive profiles that were detailed in 2023, including the Global Treasurer/CEO of GS Bank USA (Mr. Berlinski), the Chief Risk Officer (Mr. Lee), and confirmation of the PFM business divestiture. The absence of these specific titles and strategic confirmations in 2024, compared to their detailed presence in 2023, indicates significant leadership turnover and a transition away from the divested Personal Financial Management business.

key_findings.title: Capital Structure Expansion and Methodological Disclosure Changes
key_findings.analysis: Goldman Sachs expanded its capital base in early 2025 with the issuance of Series Z Preferred Stock, featuring a 6.85% fixed-rate dividend and a 2030 reset option. In risk reporting, the company removed specific disclosures regarding a Q4 2023 methodological change in assessing credit quality for U.S. residential mortgage loans (shifting from internal ratings to FICO/LTV metrics) and the quantified impact of that change. The removal of this specific credit risk methodology update suggests a stabilization or standardization of reporting practices, reducing the granularity of historical comparative adjustments in the 2024 filing.

key_findings.title: Resolution of Specific Legal Proceedings
key_findings.analysis: The 2023 filing contained specific disclosures regarding three distinct legal matters that are absent in the 2024 comparative context: (1) the voluntary dismissal of securities law class actions related to CDO market activities (M0128); (2) a preliminary settlement approval for a securities lending antitrust class action for which the firm had reserved the full amount (M0137); and (3) aluminum commodities litigation where the firm had paid its settlement contribution (M0138). The removal of these specific narratives indicates the legal exposures associated with these historical issues have been resolved or settled, thereby reducing the company's contingent liability landscape and legal risk profile for the 2024 period.

key_findings.title: Escalation of AI Risk Disclosures
key_findings.analysis: Goldman Sachs significantly expanded its AI risk disclosure in 2024 compared to 2023. While 2023 provided general warnings about AI implementation, the 2024 disclosure details specific technical and regulatory risks, including generative AI biases, privacy breaches, intellectual property infringement, and model transparency issues. It also highlights the evolving legal environment and compliance costs. This reflects an increased operational and regulatory risk profile associated with the adoption of AI technologies.

key_findings.title: Quantitative Revenue Growth and Drivers
key_findings.analysis: The company reported a 16% increase in net revenues to $53.51 billion in 2024, reversing the 2% decline from 2023 (when revenues were $46.25 billion). The 2024 growth was primarily driven by higher revenues in Global Banking & Markets (specifically Equities, Investment Banking, and FICC) and Asset & Wealth Management. This material financial shift indicates a recovery in investment banking activity and asset management fees.

key_findings.title: Introduction of Regulatory Litigation and Framework Changes
key_findings.analysis: The 2024 disclosure introduces material changes to the regulatory risk narrative regarding the Stress Capital Buffer (SCB) and CCAR framework. Unlike 2023, which focused on the static mechanics of the SCB, the 2024 filing highlights that the FRB intends to propose significant changes to the stress test framework in 2025 to reduce volatility. Furthermore, it discloses that Goldman Sachs joined a lawsuit against the FRB in December 2024 concerning inadequacies in the stress testing process, adding a layer of active legal and regulatory uncertainty to capital planning.

key_findings.title: New Constraints on Capital Distributions
key_findings.analysis: A new disclosure in 2024 explicitly details the Federal Reserve Board's (FRB) oversight mechanisms for capital distributions. It states that failure to comply with capital requirements or the need to resubmit a capital plan may limit the firm's ability to repurchase shares or pay dividends without FRB approval. This represents a new, specific constraint on shareholder returns and capital strategy that was not explicitly detailed in the prior year's disclosures.

key_findings.title: Specific Tariff and Election Outcome Risks
key_findings.analysis: The 2024 risk disclosure moves beyond general election uncertainty to cite specific policy outcomes, such as U.S. tariffs on China and proposed tariffs on trading partners. It explicitly links these geopolitical events to adverse effects on investment banking revenues, transaction volumes, and cross-border issuance, providing concrete strategic context for the impact of political changes on the firm's core business lines.

key_findings.title: Explicit AI Integration in Technology Risk
key_findings.analysis: While AI was mentioned in 2023 technology risk disclosures, the 2024 filing explicitly categorizes AI as a key emerging technology alongside distributed ledgers, requiring material resource investment. It warns that failure to integrate AI technologies as timely as competitors could result in loss of market share, service disruptions, and reduced revenues, highlighting the competitive necessity of AI adoption.

key_findings.title: Removal of Specific ACL Risk Driver Narrative
key_findings.analysis: The 2023 filing contained a specific narrative explaining the $1.97 billion increase in the Allowance for Credit Losses (ACL) in 2022, citing macroeconomic/geopolitical concerns and specific industry downgrades (TMT, real estate). The removal of this detailed driver narrative in the 2024 comparative context alters the disclosed risk narrative for that period, shifting focus away from the specific historical drivers of credit loss provisioning.

key_findings.title: Reversal in Investment Banking Performance and Drivers
key_findings.analysis: Investment banking revenues reversed a declining trend, increasing 24% to $7.74 billion in 2024 from $6.22 billion in 2023. The primary driver shifted from lower M&A activity in 2023 to higher M&A activity and significant increases in debt (leveraged finance) and equity (secondary and IPO) underwriting in 2024. This represents a material change in the Global Banking segment's performance outlook.

key_findings.title: Shift in Commissions and Fees Drivers from Prior-Year Distortions to Volume Growth
key_findings.analysis: Commissions and fees increased 8% to $4.09 billion in 2024 from $3.79 billion in 2023. The disclosure logic shifted significantly: the 2023 decline was attributed to a prior-year distortion (GreenSky impact), whereas the 2024 increase is driven by current operational performance (higher Equities market volumes and transaction fees), partially offset by losses from the GM credit card program transition. This indicates a return to organic volume-driven growth.

key_findings.title: Reversal in Net Interest Income (NII) Trend and Drivers
key_findings.analysis: Net interest income reversed from a 17% decrease in 2023 to a 27% increase in 2024, reaching $8.06 billion. In 2023, NII was pressured by rising interest expenses on liabilities (deposits, borrowings) that outpaced income gains. In 2024, the increase was driven by higher interest income from trading assets and investments due to both higher balances and rates, although this was partially offset by increased expenses in collateralized financings and deposits.

key_findings.title: Structural Change in Provision for Credit Losses Scope and Drivers
key_findings.analysis: The provision for credit losses increased to $1.35 billion in 2024 from $1.03 billion in 2023, marking a shift from a segment-specific focus (Global Banking & Markets CRE) to a firm-wide scope. The 2024 increase was primarily driven by credit card portfolio charge-offs. In contrast, 2023 provisions included credit card charge-offs and wholesale loan impairments but were partially offset by significant reserve reductions ($1.079 billion total) from the GreenSky and Marcus portfolio transactions.

key_findings.title: Reversal in Operating Expense Drivers: From Impairments to Lower Non-Recurring Costs
key_findings.analysis: Operating expenses decreased relative to 2023, driven by the absence of significant one-time charges that burdened the prior year. The 2023 increase was dominated by $1.46 billion in commercial real estate impairments, $506 million in GreenSky intangible write-downs, and $504 million in consumer goodwill impairments. The 2024 decrease reflects lower expenses in these areas, partially offset by higher compensation due to improved performance and a new $71 million FDIC special assessment fee.

key_findings.title: Significant Improvement in Asset & Wealth Management Pre-Tax Earnings
key_findings.analysis: Asset & Wealth Management reported a substantial improvement in profitability, with pre-tax earnings more than tripling to $4.55 billion in 2024 from $1.36 billion in 2023. This was achieved through a 16% increase in net revenues ($16.14 billion) driven by Equity investment gains and Management fees, combined with a 9% decrease in operating expenses ($11.83 billion) due to lower commercial real estate CIE impairments.

key_findings.title: New Strategic Target for Credit Alternative Assets
key_findings.analysis: The company introduced a new strategic objective to grow total credit alternative assets to $300 billion by the end of 2028. This disclosure, absent in the prior year, defines a clear future business priority and capital allocation strategy for the Asset & Wealth Management division.

key_findings.title: Updated Subsidiary Capital and Funding Positions
key_findings.analysis: Updated disclosures for December 2024 show changes in capital provided by Group Inc. to regulated subsidiaries compared to December 2023. Notable increases include equity invested in GS Bank USA ($56.91 billion to $62.81 billion) and GS&Co. ($36.58 billion to $38.69 billion). Conversely, unsubordinated loans decreased from $137.58 billion to $131.82 billion, and collateral/cash deposits decreased from $35.60 billion to $32.92 billion.

key_findings.title: Introduction of Platform Solutions Business Segment
key_findings.analysis: A new 'Platform Solutions' segment was disclosed, describing a distinct business line involving credit card issuance via partnership arrangements (specifically the Apple Card), raising deposits from these customers, and providing transaction banking and cash management services for corporate and institutional clients. This represents a new strategic business line not previously detailed as a separate segment.

key_findings.title: Shift in Drivers of Allowance for Credit Losses Decrease
key_findings.analysis: The drivers for the decrease in the allowance for credit losses shifted from idiosyncratic portfolio events to macroeconomic factors. In 2023, the $647 million decrease was primarily driven by reserve reductions from specific portfolio sales (GreenSky, Marcus, GM). In 2024, the $330 million decrease was driven by a reserve release in the wholesale portfolio due to an 'improved macroeconomic environment,' indicating a change in the fundamental risk dynamics of the loan book.

key_findings.title: Cessation of unsecured installment loan commitments
key_findings.analysis: In 2024, the company explicitly ceased providing commitments for unsecured installment loans, a line of consumer credit business it previously offered. This removal of a product line represents a meaningful change in business activity and revenue sources compared to the 2023 disclosure, which included these commitments alongside credit card lines.

key_findings.title: Dismissal of 1MDB-related Deferred Prosecution Agreement
key_findings.analysis: The Deferred Prosecution Agreement (DPA) with the DOJ regarding the 1MDB investigation was formally dismissed in May 2024. While the 2023 disclosure outlined the existence of this active agreement, the 2024 update reflects its completion, marking the end of significant legal obligations and regulatory uncertainty associated with the 1MDB matter.

key_findings.title: Resolution of Oak Street Health underwriting litigation
key_findings.analysis: The securities class action related to Oak Street Health offerings was resolved in December 2024 with court approval of a settlement that does not require a contribution from GS&Co. This definitive outcome removes the pending litigation risk and uncertainty associated with the case, which was previously active with a class certification motion pending in 2023.

key_findings.title: Removal of diversity goal performance metrics
key_findings.analysis: The 2024 disclosure removed detailed performance tracking against specific aspirational diversity goals (e.g., hiring percentages by demographic) that were prominently featured in the 2023 filing. Although goals expire in 2025, the removal of specific historical metrics eliminates key data for assessing progress on stated human capital objectives, representing a material shift in disclosure substance.

key_findings.title: Omission of private fund adviser rule implementation status
key_findings.analysis: The 2023 filing disclosed active compliance efforts and system enhancements required for new SEC private fund adviser rules with deadlines extending into 2025. Its absence in the 2024 matched disclosures suggests a significant shift in strategy or status regarding these regulatory burdens, warranting attention for understanding the current compliance landscape.

key_findings.title: Strategic exit signaled by removal of PFM business sale disclosure
key_findings.analysis: The disclosure regarding the sale of the Personal Financial Management (PFM) business, reported in 2023, is absent in 2024 matched disclosures. This removal indicates the business has been fully divested, representing a structural change to the company's business model and revenue streams.

key_findings.title: Discontinuation of FDIC/non-US insured deposit data
key_findings.analysis: Specific quantitative data regarding FDIC-insured deposits ($221.52B in 2023) and non-U.S. insured deposits, along with narratives about regulatory program changes affecting these figures, were removed in the 2024 filing. This eliminates transparency into a key component of liquidity stability and regulatory compliance exposure.

key_findings.title: Final resolution of U.S. Treasury securities litigation
key_findings.analysis: The disclosure regarding U.S. Treasury securities litigation, which had been dismissed and affirmed by the Second Circuit in 2024, is removed in the 2024 filing. This signifies the definitive closure of this long-standing legal exposure, eliminating associated legal uncertainty and potential appeal costs.

key_findings.title: Introduction of delayed derivative settlement risk
key_findings.analysis: A new risk factor was introduced in 2024 highlighting the risk that derivative contracts and secondary bank loans are not always confirmed or settled timely. This adds specific operational and credit risk awareness regarding counterparty delays, which was not present as a distinct disclosure in the prior year.

key_findings.title: Specific timeline added for General Motors credit card program transition
key_findings.analysis: The 2024 disclosure updated the General Motors credit card program transition agreement, specifying a concrete completion date of the third quarter of 2025. This provides a clear timeline for the strategic divestiture, whereas the previous year only noted the agreement entered into without a specific end date.

sources.text: The FRB's Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (CCAR) is designed to ensure that large BHCs, including us, have sufficient capital to permit continued operations during times of economic and financial stress.
As required by the FRB, we perform an annual capital stress test and incorporate the results into an annual capital plan, which we submit to the FRB for review.
Under the FRB's rule applicable to BHCs with $100 billion or more in total consolidated assets, including us, the SCB applies to the Standardized approach capital requirements.

The SCB reflects stressed losses estimated under the supervisory severely adverse scenario of the CCAR stress tests, as calculated by the FRB, and includes four quarters of planned common stock dividends.

The SCB, which is subject to a 2.5% floor, is generally effective on October 1 of each year and remains in effect until October 1 of the following year, unless it is reset in connection with the resubmission of a capital plan.

The SCB rule requires a BHC to receive the FRB's approval for any dividend, stock repurchase or other capital distribution, other than a capital distribution on a newly issued capital instrument, if the BHC is required to resubmit its capital plan, which may occur if the BHC determines there has been or will be a "material change" in its risk profile, financial condition or corporate structure since the plan was last submitted, or if the FRB directs the BHC to revise and resubmit its capital plan.
As part of the CCAR process, the FRB evaluates our plan to make capital distributions across a range of macroeconomic and company-specific assumptions, based on our and the FRB's own stress tests.
